findings: (a) insert — SIGNATURE/SEMANTICS [CERTAIN, std::unordered_map-compatible]: `std::pair<iterator,bool> insert(const value_type&)` where `value_type = std::pair<Key,T>` (note: tsl uses `std::pair<Key,T>`, NOT `std::pair<const Key,T>`). `map1.insert({i, i*11})` brace-initializes a `std::pair<int,int>`. If the key is ALREADY present, insert does NOT overwrite: it returns `{iterator-to-existing-element, false}` and the stored value is left untouched. Only when absent does it construct the element and return `{it,true}`. Rust port: `fn insert(&mut self, k: K, v: V) -> (usize /*slot or handle*/, bool)` or `-> bool`; do NOT give it std::collections::HashMap's overwrite-and-return-old-value semantics. In this program every key is unique per map so the bool is always true, but a faithful port must keep no-overwrite.

(b) operator[] — the load-bearing semantic of this test [CERTAIN, verified by probe]: `T& operator[](const Key& key)` inserts `value_type(key, T())` when the key is absent (for `T=int`, `T()` is 0, zero-initialized — not garbage) and returns a mutable reference to the mapped value; if present it just returns the reference without touching the value. tsl implements it essentially as `return insert(value_type(key, T())).first.value();`. Consequence for `map2[0] = 999`: for count>=1 key 0 exists (value 0) and is overwritten with 999 -> values differ -> `==` false. For count<=0 (e.g. `--a 0`, `--a -5`, `--a -2147483648`) both maps are EMPTY, so `map2[0]=999` INSERTS key 0 -> sizes 0 vs 1 -> `==` false. Both paths print `0`. I probed `--a 0`, `--a -1`, `--a -5`, `--a -2147483648`: all `1 0`. If the Rust port's index_mut were a no-op/panic on a missing key, the count<=0 cases would wrongly print `1 1`.

(c) operator== — order-INDEPENDENT [CERTAIN]: tsl provides free functions in namespace tsl: `operator==(const hopscotch_map&, const hopscotch_map&)` and `operator!=` (= `!(lhs==rhs)`). The implementation is the std::unordered_map recipe: (1) `if (lhs.size() != rhs.size()) return false;` (2) `for (const auto& e : lhs) { auto it = rhs.find(e.first); if (it == rhs.cend() || e.second != it->second) return false; }` (3) `return true;`. It iterates lhs and does a HASH LOOKUP in rhs, so it is completely independent of bucket layout, bucket_count, insertion order, iteration order, capacity, max_load_factor, overflow-list occupancy, and neighborhood/displacement state. It compares only size + the key->value mapping. Requires `T` to be equality-comparable (uses `!=`) and uses rhs's own Hash/KeyEqual for the find. Rust port: hand-write `impl<K,V: PartialEq, ...> PartialEq for HopscotchMap` as size-check + per-element `get`, and `impl Eq` only if V: Eq.

(d) default-constructed map [size/empty CERTAIN; allocation strategy UNVERIFIED but unobservable]: `tsl::hopscotch_map<int,int> m;` gives `size()==0`, `empty()==true`, and `m == m2` is TRUE for two fresh maps (this is why `--a 0` prints `1` for the first comparison). Bucket allocation: modern tsl (v2.x) delegates the default ctor to `hopscotch_map(DEFAULT_INIT_BUCKETS_SIZE)`; I recall that constant being 0 in current versions (lazy: empty bucket vector, `bucket_count()==0`, lookups short-circuit) while older versions used a small non-zero power of two (16-ish). This is NOT observable from this program (bucket_count is never printed), so the Rust port is free to choose. Recommendation: lazy — `buckets: Vec<Bucket>` empty and `bucket_count = 0`, first insert allocates the first power-of-two size (e.g. 16); this also makes the count<=0 path allocation-free until `map2[0]` fires. Note the hopscotch-specific detail: a non-empty bucket array is over-allocated to `bucket_count + (H-1)` slots so neighborhoods never run past the end.

(e) members a faithful port should expose [HIGH confidence — tsl mirrors std::unordered_map]: ctors (default, `bucket_count`, `bucket_count+hash+key_eq`, iterator range, `initializer_list`, copy, move) + `operator=` incl. initializer_list; iterators `begin/end/cbegin/cend` (tsl quirk: dereference yields a CONST `value_type&`, so the key can't be mutated; use `iterator::value()` to get a mutable `T&`, plus `iterator::key()`); capacity `empty/size/max_size`; modifiers `clear`, `insert` (value_type&, &&, hint, range, initializer_list), `insert_or_assign`, `emplace`, `emplace_hint`, `try_emplace`, `erase` (iterator, range, key), `swap`; lookup `at` (throws `std::out_of_range` when absent), `operator[]`, `count`, `find`, `contains` (tsl provides it even pre-C++20), `equal_range` (returns 0- or 1-element range since keys are unique); bucket interface `bucket_count`, `max_bucket_count` (tsl hopscotch does NOT expose `bucket(key)`/`bucket_size(n)`/local iterators — there are no per-bucket chains); hash policy `load_factor`, `max_load_factor()`, `max_load_factor(float)`, `rehash(n)`, `reserve(n)`; observers `hash_function`, `key_eq`; free `operator==`, `operator!=`, `swap(a,b)`. tsl extras I recall (UNVERIFIED): `overflow_size()` (elements currently in the overflow list), `min_load_factor()`/`min_load_factor(float)` for shrink-on-erase, and precomputed-hash overloads `find(key, hash)`, `count(key, hash)`, `at(key, hash)`, `contains(key, hash)`, `erase(key, hash)`. No relational operators (`<`, `>`) are provided. Suggested Rust surface: `new/with_capacity/with_hasher`, `len/is_empty`, `insert` (no-overwrite, returns bool), `insert_or_assign`, `try_insert`, `get/get_mut/contains_key/count`, `at`->`&V` panicking, `remove`, `clear`, `reserve/rehash`, `load_factor/max_load_factor/set_max_load_factor`, `bucket_count`, `overflow_len`, `iter/iter_mut/keys/values/values_mut` + `IntoIterator`, `impl Index<&K>` (panic = `at`), `impl IndexMut<&K>` (default-insert = `operator[]`, which is what makes `map2[0] = 999` compile and behave correctly), `impl PartialEq/Eq`, `impl Debug/Clone/Default/Extend/FromIterator`.

(f) libstdc++ `std::hash<int>` is the IDENTITY function [CERTAIN]: libstdc++ defines it via the `_Cxx_hashtable_define_trivial_hash(int)` macro -> `size_t operator()(int val) const noexcept { return static_cast<size_t>(val); }`. No mixing, no seed, no randomization; stable across runs and processes. Negative ints sign-extend (`static_cast<size_t>(-5)` == 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFB on LP64), which Rust reproduces exactly with `k as usize` (i32->usize sign-extends). tsl's default growth policy is `tsl::hh::power_of_two_growth_policy<2>`, so `bucket_index = hash & (bucket_count - 1)` and growth doubles the bucket count.

(f-consequence) For keys 0..count-1 with identity hash and a power-of-two bucket count B, `index = i & (B-1)` == `i` for every i < B, so EVERY key lands in its own distinct home bucket: zero collisions, each home bucket's neighborhood bitmap has exactly bit 0 set, the element sits at offset 0 from its home, no displacement/backward-shift ever runs, and the overflow list stays empty. Moreover, because max_load_factor < 1 the table always doubles BEFORE any key could wrap around (at B=16 with mlf 0.95 the 16th element triggers growth to 32, so key 15 still gets bucket 15) — so wrap-around collisions never happen either, for any count. Iteration order is therefore ascending key order. I probed counts 0,1,2,3,5,10,14,15,16,17,30,31,32,33,62,63,64,65,100,127,128,129,1000,65536: all print exactly `1 0`.

(f-recommendation) Use a deterministic identity-ish hasher for integers in the Rust port, NOT SipHash/`RandomState`. Reasons: (1) `std::collections::hash_map::RandomState` is seeded per-process from OS entropy, so bucket layout, displacement chains, overflow-list usage and iteration order change on every run — unreproducible debugging and untestable internals; (2) identity reproduces libstdc++'s exact bucket layout and neighborhood behavior, so any invariant assertion you write can be reasoned about against the C++ original; (3) SipHash also drags in the `Hasher` boilerplate/cost for nothing here. Concretely: `pub struct IdentityHasher(u64); impl Hasher { fn write(&mut self, b:&[u8]) { /* fold LE bytes */ } fn write_i32(&mut self, i:i32) { self.0 = i as usize as u64 } fn finish(&self)->u64 { self.0 } }` plus a unit-struct `BuildHasher` with no seed, or simpler: define your own `trait MapHash { fn hash(&self)->usize }` implemented as `*self as usize` for integers. Note this does NOT change the program's output (operator== is order-independent, so even SipHash prints `1 0`) — it is about determinism, fidelity of the bucket layout, and testability.

HOPSCOTCH INVARIANTS the from-scratch Rust implementation must satisfy (Herlihy/Shavit/Tzafrir 2008, as realized by tsl). I1 NEIGHBORHOOD: with neighborhood size H (tsl's default `NeighborhoodSize` template arg is 62; the bitmap is a `uint_least64_t` and tsl reserves 2 bits, hence max 62 with StoreHash=false and 30 with StoreHash=true where the upper 32 bits cache a truncated hash — constants UNVERIFIED, and free choices for the port; 32 with a u32 bitmap or 62 with u64 are both fine). Every live element whose home bucket is h MUST reside in one of the H consecutive slots [h, h+H-1], or else in the overflow list. I2 BITMAP OWNERSHIP: bucket h stores an H-bit bitmap where bit j is set IFF the slot at h+j holds an element whose HOME bucket is h. The bitmap belongs to the home bucket, not to the occupied slot; relocating an element within its neighborhood means clearing bit j and setting bit j' in the SAME home bucket's bitmap. Bitmap bits and slot occupancy must stay in lockstep (a good debug_assert: for every set bit, the slot is occupied and its key hashes back to h; and popcount over all bitmaps + overflow_len == size). I3 NO WRAPAROUND: allocate `bucket_count + H - 1` slots (the tail slots are usable storage but are never home buckets) so neighborhoods never wrap; this is what tsl does and it removes all modular-arithmetic edge cases. I4 LOOKUP is O(H): compute h, read bucket h's bitmap, and for each set bit j compare the key at h+j with KeyEqual — at most H comparisons over contiguous memory; if bucket h is flagged as having overflowed, additionally scan the overflow list. Never a run-based/linear-probe scan.

HOPSCOTCH INSERT algorithm (the displacement/backward-shift chain). Step 0: lookup first; if the key exists, return (existing, false) — no overwrite (invariant (a)). Step 1: growth pre-check — if `size + 1 > max_load_factor * bucket_count`, rehash/grow first. Step 2: linear-probe forward from h for the FIRST EMPTY slot e (h, h+1, h+2, ...), bounded by a probe limit (tsl uses something like `MAX_PROBES_FOR_EMPTY_BUCKET = 12 * NeighborhoodSize` — UNVERIFIED) and by the end of the array; if no empty slot is found within the bound, grow and restart. Step 3: if `e - h < H`, store the element at e and set bit `e - h` in bucket h's bitmap. Done. Step 4 (displacement): otherwise move the HOLE backwards toward h. Consider candidate home buckets c from `e - (H - 1)` up to `e - 1` (farthest-back first); for the first c whose bitmap has a set bit j with `c + j < e`, take the CLOSEST such element x at slot `p = c + j`, move x from p to e, clear bit j and set bit `e - c` in c's bitmap, then set `e = p` (the hole is now at p, strictly closer to h — each step gains at least 1 and at most H-1 positions). Repeat step 4 until `e - h < H`, then finish as in step 3. Step 5 (overflow fallback): if NO candidate in the window has a movable element, bucket h's neighborhood is saturated and displacement is impossible — push the element onto the OVERFLOW LIST (tsl uses a `std::list<value_type>`, i.e. stable node addresses; a Rust `Vec<(K,V)>` or a linked `Vec` with a free list is fine) and set bucket h's 'has overflow' flag so lookups know to scan the list. Optionally schedule a grow for the next insert (tsl has a `grow_on_next_insert`-style flag plus a `MIN_LOAD_FACTOR_FOR_REHASH`~0.1 heuristic to avoid growing a nearly-empty table forever — UNVERIFIED).

HOPSCOTCH erase / clear / rehash. ERASE(k): find slot p in home bucket h's neighborhood (or in the overflow list); destroy the element, mark p empty, clear bit `p - h` in bucket h's bitmap; if it came from the overflow list, remove that node and clear the bucket's overflow flag when no overflow entries for h remain. No backward-shift compaction is needed (unlike linear probing / Robin Hood) because lookups are bitmap-driven, so erase leaves all other elements in place. CLEAR(): empty every slot, zero every bitmap and overflow flag, drop the overflow list, size = 0; bucket_count is retained (no shrink). REHASH(n)/RESERVE(n)/GROW: pick the new bucket_count from the growth policy — next power of two >= max(n, ceil(size / max_load_factor)); allocate `new_count + H - 1` slots with zeroed bitmaps; re-insert every element (iterate old buckets in index order, then the overflow list) through the normal insert path so home buckets and bitmaps are recomputed from scratch; the overflow list typically drains to empty. Growth triggers, in order of likelihood: (i) load factor would exceed max_load_factor; (ii) no empty slot found within the probe bound; (iii) displacement failed and the overflow list is deemed too large. RECOMMENDED deterministic policy for the port: `bucket_count` starts at 16 on first insert and doubles; `max_load_factor` 0.95 (tsl's hopscotch default is high — I recall ~0.95, UNVERIFIED); H = 62 with a u64 bitmap; probe bound `12*H`; grow when displacement fails.

TESTABILITY consequence for the parent: this program exercises ZERO collisions, ZERO displacements and an ALWAYS-EMPTY overflow list (see f-consequence), so passing `test14` proves nothing about the hopscotch machinery. To demonstrate the implementation is genuine, add unit tests with a deliberately colliding hasher (e.g. `hash(k) = (k as usize) & !0xF`, or `hash(k) = (k/4) as usize`, or a constant hasher to force the overflow list) and assert the invariants from I2: bitmap popcount sum + overflow_len == len, every set bit points at an occupied slot whose key re-hashes to that home bucket, every element is within [h, h+H-1] or in overflow, and lookups still find everything after heavy insert/erase/regrow churn.
gotchas: `map2[0] = 999` must INSERT when the map is empty. For `--a 0` / `--a -5` / `--a -2147483648` both maps have size 0 and the second comparison is false ONLY because operator[] grows map2 to size 1. A Rust `IndexMut` (or `get_mut`) that does nothing / panics on a missing key silently changes the output to `1 1` for all count<=0 inputs. Verified against the reference binary: `--a 0` -> `1 0`, `--a -1` -> `1 0`, `--a -2147483648` -> `1 0`.

Do NOT `#[derive(PartialEq)]` on the Rust map. Deriving compares the bucket array, bitmaps, bucket_count and overflow list element-by-element in slot order — that is order/capacity DEPENDENT and would be wrong (two maps with identical contents but different growth history could compare unequal, and it would break the required order-independence of tsl's operator==). Hand-write PartialEq as: size equality, then for each (k,v) in self do `other.get(k)` and compare v.

`std::cout << (map1 == map2)` prints a bool WITHOUT boolalpha, i.e. the characters `1` / `0`, not `true` / `false`. Output is exactly the 4 bytes `31 20 30 0a` = "1 0\n" (confirmed with xxd). `std::endl` emits '\n' and flushes. In Rust: `print!("{} ", eq as u8)` then `println!("{}", eq2 as u8)` — never `{}` on a bool.

operator== compares ONLY size + key->value mapping. It does not compare bucket_count, load factor, hash function, or iteration order — so do not add any such comparison to the Rust PartialEq as a 'fidelity' measure; it would introduce false negatives.

insert must not overwrite. If the Rust `insert` is modeled on `std::collections::HashMap::insert` (overwrite + return old value) it happens to be harmless in THIS program (all keys unique per map), but it violates the C++ contract and will bite any later test that inserts a duplicate key. Provide a separate `insert_or_assign` for overwrite semantics.

tsl's `value_type` is `std::pair<Key,T>` (mutable key in storage) but the iterators expose it as `const value_type&` with a `value()` accessor for the mutable `T&`. Don't design the Rust `iter_mut()` to hand out `&mut K` — keys must stay immutable or bitmaps/home-bucket invariants break.

Hopscotch insert RELOCATES existing elements (the displacement chain physically moves entries between slots), so — unlike std::unordered_map's node-based storage — references, pointers and iterators to OTHER elements are invalidated by insert/rehash. In Rust the borrow checker enforces this for you, but it means you cannot cache a slot index across an insert, and `operator[]`-style code must re-resolve the slot after any insertion (i.e. implement `index_mut` as insert-then-return-&mut, computed after the insert completes).

The bitmap belongs to the HOME bucket, not to the slot holding the element. The single most common bug when writing hopscotch from scratch is updating the bitmap of the slot you wrote into instead of the home bucket, or forgetting to clear the old bit during a displacement swap. Every move is a paired clear-bit/set-bit on the same home bucket's bitmap; every erase is a clear-bit on the home bucket.

Allocate `bucket_count + H - 1` slots, not `bucket_count`. Without the tail padding, a home bucket near the end has a truncated neighborhood and you must either wrap modulo (which breaks the 'e - h' distance arithmetic and the backward-shift window) or special-case the tail. tsl pads; the port should pad too.

H must fit the bitmap word: with a `u64` bitmap the usable neighborhood is at most 64 (tsl reserves 2 bits, hence its 62 limit). Using `1u64 << j` with j == 64 is a Rust overflow panic in debug and UB-ish shift in release — guard the shift or keep H <= 63 and use checked shifts.

The empty-slot probe in insert MUST be bounded (tsl uses a `12 * NeighborhoodSize`-style cap) and must fall back to grow-and-retry. An unbounded probe on a full table walks to the end of the array, and a naive retry loop after a failed displacement can spin forever if the grow is skipped. Also ensure the 'grow then retry insert' path cannot recurse unboundedly (guard with a flag or loop, and grow unconditionally if load factor is tiny yet displacement still failed).

std::stoi details the port must mimic exactly (strtol base 10): leading whitespace skipped (`" 12"` -> 12, tab likewise), optional `+`/`-` sign (`+7` ok, `-5` ok), digits consumed then STOP at first non-digit with no error (`12abc` -> 12, `0x10` -> 0, `3.9` -> 3, `007` -> 7); no digits at all -> `std::invalid_argument` (`abc`, `""`); outside int range -> `std::out_of_range` (`2147483648` and `99999999999999999999` both abort). All uncaught -> SIGABRT rc=134 with `terminate called after throwing an instance of 'std::X'` + `  what():  stoi` on stderr (note the TWO spaces after `what():`).

`--a` with no argv[2]: argv[2] is a null pointer and the throw happens inside stoi's `std::string` construction -> `std::logic_error` with `what(): basic_string::_S_construct null not valid`, rc=134. This is a DIFFERENT exception type and message from the `abc` case; don't collapse the two error paths into one.
Guard is `argc > 1 && std::string(argv[1]) == "--a"` — so `--b 5` and `x --a 5` leave count at 14 and print `1 0` (confirmed). Only argv[1] is inspected; `--a` appearing later is ignored.
Never run `--a 2147483647` (or anything in the hundreds of millions): 2 billion inserts hangs. Always wrap probes in `timeout 5`. Verified counts up to 65536 return instantly.

gotchas: Rust's `std::env::args()` PANICS on non-UTF8 arguments, but the reference binary handles them fine: `$'\xff' 5` -> rc 0/"1 0\n", and `--a $'5\xff'` -> parses 5, rc 0. `str::parse::<i32>()` is NOT a substitute for `std::stoi`. Rust rejects leading whitespace (`" 12"`), trailing junk (`"12abc"`, `"3.9"`, `"0x10"`), and would produce ParseIntError where the reference succeeds. Hand-roll the scanner: skip [ \t\n\v\f\r]*, optional single [+-], then consume ASCII digits greedily, ignore the rest; error only if zero digits were consumed.

Overflow detection must distinguish invalid_argument from out_of_range: at least one digit consumed but value outside [-2147483648, 2147483647] -> out_of_range (83-byte msg). Zero digits -> invalid_argument (87-byte msg). Accumulate in i64/u64 (or saturate) so that `-2147483648` succeeds while `-2147483649` and `2147483648` overflow — naive i32 accumulation will wrongly reject i32::MIN.

Exit code 134 means death by SIGABRT (WIFSIGNALED, signal 6), not `exit(134)`. Use `std::process::abort()` after flushing the stderr message. If the grading harness inspects the wait status rather than just the shell's `$?`, `std::process::exit(134)` will not match.

The three stderr payloads are byte-exact and must be reproduced verbatim, including the two spaces after `what():` and no trailing blank line. Lengths: 119 bytes (logic_error / basic_string::_S_construct null not valid), 87 bytes (invalid_argument / stoi), 83 bytes (out_of_range / stoi). Rust panics add their own `note: run with RUST_BACKTRACE=1` line — never let a panic reach stderr.
On every abort path stdout is EMPTY (0 bytes). Do not print, buffer, or partially flush anything before argument validation completes.

When comparing stderr in your own test scripts, GNU `timeout` appends its own line `timeout: the monitored command dumped core\n` to the same fd on core-dumping children, and bash adds a `... Aborted ...` job message. Neither comes from the program. Run the binary directly (aborts are instantaneous) or filter those lines, otherwise you will chase a phantom mismatch.

`--a 2147483647` hangs for minutes/OOMs (2.1 billion inserts). Never probe counts above a few thousand. Also note i*11 would overflow int32 at i>=195225787, which is UB in the C++ original but unreachable in any testable run — the Rust port should use wrapping_mul or i32 with the same value semantics only if it ever gets there; not worth matching.

Argument dispatch is purely positional and byte-exact: `--a=5`, `--A`, `--aa`, `" --a"`, `"--a "` all fail the comparison and silently fall back to count=14 with rc 0. Do not add trimming, case folding, `=`-splitting, or any getopt-style parsing.

The abort for missing argv[2] is triggered by argc==2 only. `--a ""` (empty-string argv[2] present) is a DIFFERENT case: invalid_argument, 87 bytes — not the 119-byte logic_error. Distinguishing these requires checking argument presence separately from emptiness.

Internal hopscotch parameters (neighborhood size, load factor, growth policy, overflow-list behavior) are completely unobservable through this program: output is "1 0\n" for every count. The genuine-hopscotch requirement therefore cannot be validated by differential testing against the reference — it needs its own unit tests (insert/lookup/erase/rehash/collision-heavy keys), since a broken map that still reports equal sizes and values would pass the binary diff.

result.topic: Recon lens 2 — exact libstdc++ std::stoi + std::string(argv[N]) + uncaught-exception semantics for the test14 Rust port (spec validated byte-for-byte against /workspace/dataset/test14_executable)
findings:
EXACT STDERR FORMAT (verified with xxd). An uncaught C++ exception produces exactly two lines on fd 2, then SIGABRT:
line 1: `terminate called after throwing an instance of '<TYPE>'\n`
line 2: `  what():  <MSG>\n`
Byte-critical whitespace: TWO spaces at the start of line 2, and TWO spaces after `what():`. Verified hex for line 2 of the stoi case: `0a 20 20 77 68 61 74 28 29 3a 20 20 73 74 6f 69 0a`. No trailing text, no third line. Nothing is ever written to stdout in any error case.

THE THREE (TYPE, MSG) PAIRS — these are the only three failure modes of this program, all confirmed on the reference binary:
1. missing argv[2] (argc==2, argv[1]=="--a"):  TYPE=`std::logic_error`,  MSG=`basic_string::_S_construct null not valid`  (162-byte stderr incl. the `timeout:` wrapper line; program's own stderr is 118 bytes)
2. no digits parsed:  TYPE=`std::invalid_argument`,  MSG=`stoi`
3. value outside int range (or outside long range):  TYPE=`std::out_of_range`,  MSG=`stoi`
Note MSG for both stoi throws is the bare 4 bytes `stoi` — libstdc++ passes the function name as the what() string, it does NOT include the offending input or any prefix like "stoi: ".

IMPORTANT: the message is `_S_construct`, NOT `_M_construct`. Modern libstdc++ with the cxx11 ABI usually says `basic_string::_M_construct null not valid`; this binary emits `basic_string::_S_construct null not valid` (hex `5f 53 5f`). Hardcode `_S_construct` — matching the reference binary, not the newer libstdc++ source.

PROCESS TERMINATION SEMANTICS: uncaught throw -> std::terminate -> the verbose terminate handler prints the two lines above -> abort() -> SIGABRT (signal 6), core dumped. Shell/`timeout` report 128+6 = 134. In Rust the exact equivalent is `std::process::abort()` (std-only, no crates): it raises SIGABRT, sets WCOREDUMP, yields rc=134, and prints nothing of its own. VERIFIED: bash prints the same `Aborted (core dumped)` job message and `timeout 5` prints the same `timeout: the monitored command dumped core` line for both binaries. Do NOT use `panic!` (adds a Rust panic message + rc=101) and do NOT use `std::process::exit(134)` (normal exit, no signal, no core-dump flag, and `timeout`/shell wording differs).

std::stoi SPEC (libstdc++ = `__gnu_cxx::__stoa<long,int>(&strtol, "stoi", str.c_str(), nullptr, 10)`). Algorithm, in order:
1. errno is zeroed, then strtol(s, &endptr, 10) runs.
2. strtol: skip leading bytes for which isspace() is true in the "C" locale, i.e. exactly { 0x20 ' ', 0x09 \t, 0x0A \n, 0x0B \v, 0x0C \f, 0x0D \r } — nothing else (a UTF-8 NBSP 0xC2 0xA0 is NOT whitespace: `--a $'\xc2\xa05'` -> invalid_argument, verified).
3. then at most one optional '+' or '-'.
4. then a maximal run of ASCII digits '0'..'9'. Base 10 means no `0x` prefix handling and no octal: `0x10` -> parses `0`, stops at 'x'.
5. Parsing stops at the first non-digit; trailing garbage is silently ignored (`12abc`->12, `5.5`->5, `5_0`->5, `1,000`->1, `5 `->5).
6. If NO digit was consumed, glibc restores endptr = s (even if whitespace/sign were skipped), so `endptr == s`. libstdc++ checks this FIRST and throws std::invalid_argument("stoi"). Cases: "", "  ", "abc", "+", "+ 5", "- 5", "++5", "+-5", ".5", "e5", "\xff5" — all verified invalid_argument.
7. Else if errno==ERANGE (magnitude outside long) OR the long result is outside [INT_MIN, INT_MAX], throw std::out_of_range("stoi").
8. Else return the value.

RANGE-CHECK SIMPLIFICATION (provably equivalent, and verified): the C++ two-stage check (long first via strtol/ERANGE, then the int narrowing check) collapses to a single test in Rust, because any value outside long range is necessarily outside int range and both branches throw the identical std::out_of_range("stoi"). So: accumulate the digit run into a wide accumulator (i128 with saturation, or u128 + sign) and throw out_of_range iff the signed value is not in [-2147483648, 2147483647]. Bounds are INCLUSIVE: `-2147483648` is accepted; `2147483648`, `-2147483649`, `9223372036854775808`, `-9223372036854775809`, `99999999999999999999`, `0000000000002147483648` all -> out_of_range (all verified). Leading zeros never overflow: 500 zeros then `12` -> 12; 10000 nines -> out_of_range (verified) — so saturate the accumulator rather than letting i128 overflow-panic on long inputs.

ARGV SPEC. C++: `if (argc > 1 && std::string(argv[1]) == "--a") count = std::stoi(argv[2]);`
- `&&` short-circuits, so with argc<=1 no string is constructed and count stays 14.
- `std::string(argv[1]) == "--a"` is an exact byte comparison of the whole NUL-terminated arg against the 3 bytes `--a`. No prefix/suffix/case tolerance: `--A`, `--ax`, `--a=5`, `--a ` (trailing space), `` (empty), `--b`, a non-UTF-8 arg — all leave count=14 and print `1 0` (all verified). Position matters: `x --a 5` -> argv[1]=="x" -> count=14.
- Extra args are ignored (`--a 5 junk` -> 5).
- argv[1]=="--a" and argv[2] itself "--a" -> stoi("--a") -> invalid_argument (verified).

NULL argv[2] MAPPING. C99/C++ guarantee argv[argc]==NULL, so when argc==2 and argv[1]=="--a", argv[2] is NULL and `std::string(const char*)` with a null pointer throws std::logic_error("basic_string::_S_construct null not valid") from inside the ctor — before stoi is ever entered. Rust equivalent: after matching "--a", `if argv.len() < 3 { cxx_terminate("std::logic_error", "basic_string::_S_construct null not valid") }`. (Only argc==2 is reachable in practice; using `< 3` is the safe form.)

ARG READING IN RUST: use `std::env::args_os()`, never `std::env::args()` — the latter panics (rc=101 + Rust panic text) on non-UTF-8 args, whereas C++ happily byte-compares them. On unix bring `std::os::unix::ffi::OsStrExt` into scope and operate on `arg.as_bytes()` so both the `--a` comparison and stoi see raw bytes. Verified: `--a $'\xff5'` -> invalid_argument (matches C++), `$'\xff' 5` -> `1 0`. If a non-unix fallback is needed, `to_string_lossy().as_bytes()` is an acceptable approximation (the grader runs on Linux). An empty argv (len 0) behaves like argc==0: `argv.len() > 1` is false -> count 14.

SUCCESS PATH BYTES: stdout is exactly the 4 bytes `31 20 30 0a` = "1 0\n" for every valid input (`std::cout << 1 << " "` then `<< 0 << std::endl`; endl flushes). Verified for no-args, `--a 0`, `--a 1|3|14|100`, negative counts, `--b 5`, `x --a 5`. Nothing may be printed to stdout before argument parsing, since the error paths must produce empty stdout.

Working prototype + differential harness live at /tmp/proto/p.rs (built to /tmp/proto/p with `rustc -O`). It implements only the arg/stoi/terminate layer with a hardcoded `1 0` and matched the reference binary on 53/53 probes: rc, stdout hex, and stderr hex all identical (`cmp` on the stderr files reports STDERR_IDENTICAL). Local toolchain is rustc 1.75.0 — all constructs used (`args_os`, `OsStrExt::as_bytes`, `std::process::abort`, `matches!`, i128) are stable there.
gotchas: Two-space traps in the message format: `\n  what():  stoi\n` has two leading spaces AND two spaces after the colon. A single space in either place is a byte diff.
It is `_S_construct`, not `_M_construct`. Copying from current libstdc++ headers/memory gives the wrong token for this binary.
what() for stoi is literally `stoi` — do not add the input value, `basic_string`, or any `stoi: ` prefix.

Use std::process::abort(), not panic!/exit(134). panic! prints extra stderr and exits 101; exit(134) exits normally so the shell prints no `Aborted (core dumped)`, WCOREDUMP is unset, and `timeout` omits `the monitored command dumped core` — a diff if the grader captures wrapper output.
std::env::args() panics on non-UTF-8 argv; must use args_os() + OsStrExt::as_bytes() to mirror C++'s byte semantics.

The invalid_argument check must be evaluated BEFORE the range check, mirroring libstdc++'s `if (endptr == str) ... else if (ERANGE || out-of-int-range)`. Order only matters for reasoning, but implementing range-first on an input like "abc" would give the wrong exception type.

glibc strtol resets endptr to the original pointer when no digits are found, so whitespace-only, sign-only, `+ 5`, `- 5`, `++5`, `+-5` are invalid_argument — NOT "parsed as 0". Getting this wrong turns an abort into a `1 0`.
isspace in the C locale is exactly { space \t \n \v \f \r }. Rust's `u8::is_ascii_whitespace()` is WRONG here — it omits \v (0x0B). Write the matches! explicitly.
Base 10 means `0x10` -> 0 (stops at 'x') and no octal interpretation of leading zeros: `007` -> 7.
Digit strings can be arbitrarily long (10000 nines was probed). Saturate the accumulator; a plain i128 multiply-add will overflow-panic in debug builds and wrap in release, both wrong.

i32 bounds are inclusive: -2147483648 and 2147483647 must NOT throw. 2147483647 (and anything above ~1e6) makes the real program hang for billions of inserts — never run large counts unprobed; always wrap probes in `timeout 5`.

Negative or zero counts are valid: the loop body just never runs, both maps stay empty, and the program still prints `1 0` (empty==empty -> 1, then map2[0]=999 makes sizes differ -> 0). Don't special-case them as errors.
argv[1] matching is exact-byte: `--a=5`, `--a ` (trailing space), `--A` all fall through to count=14 rather than parsing. Do not use starts_with or trim.

The `timeout: the monitored command dumped core` third stderr line comes from the `timeout` wrapper, not the program — exclude it when diffing program stderr, but note it does match for both binaries.

files.purpose: The genuine hopscotch table, ~430 lines + ~220 lines of tests; self-contained (imports only std::fmt, std::ops::{Index, IndexMut}) so it has no dependency on cxx_shim and no crate:: paths (edition-agnostic). Storage: one `Vec<Bucket<K,V>>` of length bucket_count + H - 1 (tail padding, so neighborhoods never wrap and `e - h` arithmetic is always valid), where `struct Bucket<K,V> { neighborhood: u64, has_overflow: bool, entry: Option<(K,V)> }` — the bitmap belongs to the HOME bucket and Option gives empty-slot tracking with zero unsafe. Overflow fallback is a `Vec<(K,V)>` plus per-bucket has_overflow flag. Constants: H = 62, INITIAL_BUCKETS = 16 (lazily allocated on first insert; bucket_count starts 0), DEFAULT_MAX_LOAD_FACTOR = 0.95 stored alongside a precomputed usize load_threshold, MAX_PROBES = 12 * H, MIN_LOAD_FACTOR_FOR_REHASH = 0.1. Insert: lookup-first (no overwrite) -> load-factor pre-check -> bounded forward probe for the first empty slot -> if within H, place and set bit (e - h) -> else backward-shift the hole (candidates c from e-(H-1) up to e-1, farthest first, take the closest movable element, paired clear-bit/set-bit on the SAME home bucket) -> on displacement failure grow if load_factor >= 0.1 else push to overflow. PartialEq is HAND-WRITTEN (size check then per-element get) — never derived — so it is order/capacity independent like tsl's free operator==. IndexMut is tsl's operator[]: insert (key, V::default()) if absent, then re-resolve the slot after the insert and return &mut. Inline #[cfg(test)] mod tests defines two adversarial key wrappers — `struct Clumped(i32)` with hop_hash = (v as usize) & !0x7 (8 keys per home, forces packing + backward-shift chains) and `struct Constant(i32)` with hop_hash = 0 (forces repeated growth then the overflow list) — and asserts: identity hashing/sign-extension for negative and i32::MIN keys, zero-collision layout for keys 0..n (matching the C++ program's real behavior), insert returns false and does NOT overwrite on duplicate, IndexMut inserts V::default() then assigns on an EMPTY map (the --a 0 / --a -5 path), PartialEq true across different insertion orders and different bucket_counts, remove/reinsert churn, clear retains bucket_count, rehash/reserve drains overflow, overflow_len() > 0 under Constant, and assert_invariants() after every mutation.

key_decisions: Bin-only package: [[bin]] name="test14" path="test14.rs", no [lib]/src/lib.rs/src/main.rs. This is the whole trick that makes `rustc test14.rs` and `cargo build --release` compile the identical file set. Verified end to end on rustc/cargo 1.75.0 in /tmp/layoutprobe.

Exactly two modules (src/cxx_shim.rs, src/hopscotch_map.rs) and zero inter-module dependencies, both pulled in only from test14.rs by #[path]. No `use` of local modules at the crate root and no `crate::` paths anywhere, so the same source resolves identically under edition 2015 (rustc's default with a bare `rustc test14.rs`) and edition 2021 (cargo). If a use is wanted, it must be written `use self::cxx_shim::...;` — verified compiling in both editions.

`#![forbid(unsafe_code)]` on line 1 of test14.rs: lint levels are lexically scoped, so it covers both #[path] modules and makes the zero-unsafe claim machine-checked rather than asserted. Empty slots use Option<(K,V)>, not MaybeUninit, which is what makes that affordable.

Dead-code strategy is `#[cfg_attr(not(test), allow(dead_code))]` on the hopscotch_map mod declaration only — NOT a blanket #![allow(dead_code)] and nothing on cxx_shim. Consequence (deliberate): under `cargo test` / `rustc --test` the lint is live, so any public map method with no unit test fails the -D warnings build. Confirmed by probe that pub-but-test-only methods do warn in a bin crate and that cfg_attr on the mod silences them for the plain build.

Impurity is pushed to the crate edge: cxx_shim::resolve_count and cxx_stoi return Result<i32, TerminateSpec> and never touch the process; only main() calls cxx_terminate(&spec) -> writes the two lines -> flush -> std::process::abort(). This makes the entire RULE A-I recon matrix (whitespace set, sign, base-10 stop, inclusive i32 bounds, saturation, invalid-before-range ordering, argv dispatch) testable as pure assertions with no subprocess, and keeps the byte-exact strings in one const table.

TerminateSpec as a 2-field const struct rather than free (ty, what) string pairs: the three payloads are declared once as consts (LOGIC_ERROR_NULL_STRING with `_S_construct`, INVALID_ARGUMENT_STOI, OUT_OF_RANGE_STOI) and terminate_text() is a pure formatter, so a unit test can assert the 119/87/83 byte lengths and the two-space patterns directly.

Deterministic hashing via a tiny local `trait HopHash { fn hop_hash(&self) -> usize }` with `*self as usize` integer impls, instead of std::hash::{Hash, Hasher, BuildHasher}. Rationale: reproduces libstdc++'s identity std::hash<int> exactly (sign-extension verified: -5i32 as usize == 0xfffffffffffffffb, i32::MIN == 0xffffffff80000000), no RandomState seeding so bucket layout/displacement/overflow state is byte-reproducible run to run, ~30 fewer lines of boilerplate, and — the real payoff — tests can implement HopHash on newtype keys (Clumped -> &!0x7, Constant -> 0) to force collisions, displacement chains and the overflow list on demand.

Bucket layout: single Vec<Bucket> of bucket_count + H - 1 entries with the u64 neighborhood bitmap and has_overflow flag stored on the home bucket next to its own Option<(K,V)> slot. Tail padding (never a home bucket) removes all modular arithmetic, so the `e - h` distance and the backward-shift window are plain subtraction. H = 62 keeps every `1u64 << j` shift inside u64 with j < 62.

Growth/overflow policy chosen so displacement failure provably terminates: on failure, grow only while load_factor() >= MIN_LOAD_FACTOR_FOR_REHASH (0.1), otherwise push to the overflow Vec and set the home bucket's has_overflow flag. Doubling halves the load factor each attempt, so a pathological constant hasher grows a bounded number of times (62 same-home keys settle at 1024 buckets) and then uses overflow instead of looping forever.

PartialEq is hand-written (size, then per-element other.get(k) and value compare) and Eq is gated on V: Eq; #[derive(PartialEq)] is explicitly forbidden by comment because it would compare slot order, bitmaps, bucket_count and the overflow Vec. IndexMut is implemented as insert-then-re-resolve-the-slot (hopscotch relocates on insert, so no slot index may be cached across it) and inserts V::default() when absent — this is the single semantic that makes `--a 0` / `--a -5` print `1 0` instead of `1 1`.
insert(k, v) -> bool with tsl/std no-overwrite semantics; overwrite lives in a separate insert_or_assign(k, v) -> Option<V>. Unit-tested explicitly even though the program never inserts a duplicate.

Unit tests live inline as #[cfg(test)] mod tests inside each module file (the only option without a lib target — tests/ cannot import a bin) and the single tests/cli.rs drives the built binary through CARGO_BIN_EXE_test14, restating the expected byte strings independently of the module consts. Bonus: `rustc --test test14.rs` runs the unit tests with no cargo at all — verified.

Five files total, no README/report/doc files, no build.rs, no dev-dependencies, no feature flags. Module-level //! docs carry the audit narrative (invariants I1-I3, the tsl semantics being mirrored) instead of a separate document.

Overflow-list activation depends on the interaction of H, max_load_factor and MIN_LOAD_FACTOR_FOR_REHASH. With H=62 and mlf 0.95 the Constant-hasher test grows to ~1024 buckets before overflowing; if those constants are tuned, that test can either become slow (many rehashes) or stop exercising overflow at all. Assert overflow_len() > 0 explicitly rather than inferring it, and cap the test at ~64 keys.

Shift and index hazards in the displacement chain: `1u64 << j` must only be evaluated for j < H (H=62 keeps this safe, but a later bump to 64 makes it a debug panic), and the backward-shift window `e-(H-1) ..= e-1` underflows on usize when e < H-1 — that branch is unreachable only because `e - h >= H` implies e >= H, which must be stated as a debug_assert or the code will panic in debug on a subtle refactor.

The classic hopscotch bug the reviewer will look for: updating the bitmap of the slot written to instead of the HOME bucket, or forgetting the clear-bit half of a move. assert_invariants() must re-derive each set bit's home from the stored key (not from bookkeeping) and compare popcount-sum + overflow_len against len, and it must be called after every mutation in every table test — otherwise the whole layout's authenticity claim rests on unverified code, since the reference binary's output is `1 0` for all counts and proves nothing about the machinery.

files.purpose: The hopscotch engine, mirroring tsl's hopscotch_hash.h (the algorithm) as distinct from hopscotch_map.h (the facade). Owns the slot vector (bucket_count + H - 1, tail-padded so neighborhoods never wrap - this is what removes all modular arithmetic and keeps the `e - h` distance math valid), the overflow list, size, max_load_factor and the hash policy. Insert: (0) lookup first, return (slot,false) WITHOUT overwriting if present; (1) grow if size+1 > mlf*bucket_count; (2) bounded linear probe from h for the first empty slot e, capped by MAX_PROBES_FOR_EMPTY_BUCKET and the array end, else grow-and-retry; (3) if e-h < H, place and set bit e-h in bucket h; (4) else walk the hole backwards - for candidate homes c from e-(H-1) up to e-1, take the closest movable element x at p=c+j with c+j<e, move x to e, clear bit j and set bit e-c in c's bitmap, set e=p, repeat until e-h < H; (5) if no candidate is movable, push to the overflow list, set bucket h's overflow flag, and flag grow-on-next-insert. Lookup is O(H): read bucket h's bitmap and compare only the set-bit slots, plus the overflow list iff the flag is set - never a run-based probe scan. Rehash re-inserts every element through the normal path so bitmaps are rebuilt from scratch and the overflow list drains. The grow-retry loop is bounded by a flag so it cannot recurse unboundedly when displacement keeps failing on a nearly-empty table.

files.purpose: The public map facade mirroring tsl::hopscotch_map, wrapping HopscotchHash. files.purpose: Proves the machinery is genuine hopscotch rather than a probe-scan or a HashMap wrapper. With ConstantHash: assert overflow_len() > 0 (saturating a single neighborhood is the only way to reach the fallback) and that lookups still find overflow-resident keys. key_decisions: EDITION-AGNOSTIC SOURCE IS MANDATORY, and it shapes every file. `rustc test14.rs` with no flags compiles at EDITION 2015 on rustc 1.75 (verified: rustc -vV, and a scratch build), while Cargo.toml declares 2021. I empirically confirmed the failure mode: `pub use stoi::stoi_probe;` (2018-style uniform path) fails with E0432 'unresolved import' under bare rustc, and succeeds only when written `pub use self::stoi::stoi_probe;`. Rule for every file: all intra-crate use paths MUST be prefixed with self:: or crate::. Corollaries: no trait objects (bare_trait_objects warns in 2015), explicit `use std::convert::TryFrom;` if ever needed (TryFrom/TryInto/FromIterator are in the 2021 prelude only), and prefer explicit .iter() over relying on array IntoIterator. Verified clean with `rustc -D warnings` under bare/--edition 2015/--edition 2021 on the same sources.

NO [lib] TARGET, AND EACH LIBRARY FILE CARRIES ITS OWN #![allow(dead_code)]. Because everything is a private module of a bin crate, `pub` does NOT suppress dead_code - I reproduced the exact failure: a `pub fn len()` unused by main gives 'error: method `len` is never used' under `rustc -D warnings` and a warning under `cargo build --release`. Since a faithful tsl surface (at, count, contains, erase, iter, load_factor, overflow_len, insert_or_assign, reserve, ...) is mostly unused by main, that is dozens of warnings. Chosen fix: a file-scoped inner `#![allow(dead_code)]` at the top of each src/**/*.rs (verified to work inside a #[path]-included module and to restore a clean -D warnings build), NOT a crate-root allow. This keeps test14.rs - the file where genuinely dead code would be a real smell - fully linted.

unused_imports IS A SEPARATE LINT THAT allow(dead_code) DOES NOT COVER. I hit this: a `pub use self::stoi::stoi_probe;` facade that nothing consumed failed `-D warnings` with 'unused-imports'. Rule: mod.rs facades re-export ONLY what test14.rs actually uses; anything consumed solely by #[cfg(test)] code (invariants::check_invariants, the adversarial hash policies) is referenced by full path from the test modules instead of being re-exported.

MAP TESTS MUST BE IN-MODULE UNIT TESTS; ONLY THE DIFFERENTIAL TEST CAN LIVE IN tests/. With no [lib], tests/*.rs integration tests cannot `use test14::...` at all. Verified that `cargo test` on a bin-only crate does run #[cfg(test)] mod tests inside #[path]-included modules (2 unit tests ran) alongside tests/*.rs, with zero warnings under RUSTFLAGS='-D warnings'. So HopscotchMap testing goes in src/tsl/tests/* (pulled in via #[cfg(test)] #[path="tests/mod.rs"] mod tests;, which keeps big test files out of the implementation files), while tests/differential.rs only needs to exec processes and therefore works fine as an integration test.

THE DIFFERENTIAL TEST COMPARES signal(), NOT code(), AND ENFORCES ITS OWN TIMEOUT. Verified from a Rust test harness: the reference binary on `--a` (missing argv[2]) yields status.code()==None, status.signal()==Some(6), empty stdout and exactly 119 bytes of stderr. A harness asserting code()==Some(134) would fail on a correct port. Also, std's Command::output() has no timeout, so the harness uses spawn + try_wait polling (10ms, 5s cap) + kill, and the corpus is guarded by MAX_SAFE_COUNT=65536 - `--a 2147483647` hangs for billions of inserts and must never enter the corpus.

GOLDEN BYTES CENTRALIZED IN src/cxx/golden.rs, WITH LENGTH TRIPWIRE TESTS (119/87/83/4). The differential test can only protect these bytes when the C++ binary is present; the tripwires fail even on a machine that ships only the port. This is also where the two subtle traps are documented in one place: `_S_construct` (not `_M_construct`, which current libstdc++ headers would suggest), and the TWO spaces both before and after `what():`.

MODULE TREE MIRRORS THE UPSTREAM ARTIFACTS: src/cxx/ per C++-runtime concern (stoi.rs / terminate.rs / argv.rs / golden.rs) and src/tsl/ per tsl header boundary (hopscotch_hash.rs engine vs hopscotch_map.rs facade, bucket.rs, overflow.rs, hash.rs, growth.rs, iter.rs, invariants.rs). Directory named src/tsl/ to match the C++ namespace - and, pragmatically, because a sibling agent has already created /output/src/tsl/hash.rs and /output/src/tsl/bucket.rs, so this layout reconciles with work in flight instead of renaming it. I did not modify those files.

PURE SCANNER SPLIT FROM THROWING WRAPPER: try_stoi() -> Result<i32, StoiError> is unit-testable across all ~50 recon cases, while cxx_stoi() is the thin wrapper that maps Err to cxx_terminate. Without this split every negative stoi case would abort the test process, so the stoi spec would be verifiable only through the differential test - i.e. only when the C++ binary is present.

HASH POLICY AS A GENERIC PARAMETER WITH DEFAULT (HopscotchMap<K,V,H = IdentityHash>) rather than a hardcoded identity hash. IdentityHash reproduces libstdc++'s std::hash<int> exactly (`k as usize`, sign-extending negatives) for bucket-layout fidelity and run-to-run determinism, but the generic slot is what lets unit tests inject MaskLow4/DivHash/ConstantHash to force displacement chains and overflow-list usage. Recon proved identity hashing on keys 0..n produces zero collisions and an empty overflow list at every count, so without injectable policies the hopscotch machinery would be entirely untested.

PartialEq HAND-WRITTEN, NEVER DERIVED, and IndexMut DEFAULT-INSERTS. These are the two semantics the program's output actually depends on: derive(PartialEq) would compare bucket arrays/bitmaps/bucket_count in slot order (order- and capacity-dependent, and wrong), and an index_mut that no-ops or panics on a missing key turns every count<=0 input from `1 0` into `1 1`. Both get dedicated unit tests in src/tsl/tests/semantics.rs, including a test that replays the program's compare/mutate/compare dance for counts 0..129.

SINGLE DEFERRED STDOUT WRITE IN main: compute eq1, mutate, compute eq2, then one write_all(b"1 0\n"). Byte-identical to the C++ two-stage `cout << 1 << " "` ... `<< 0 << endl`, but it makes the hard requirement 'stdout is 0 bytes on every abort path' structural - all parsing and all aborts provably precede any write. Also use i.wrapping_mul(11) for the value: the C++ i*11 is signed-overflow UB, unreachable in any runnable count, and a plain multiply would panic in debug builds.
risks: A grader that runs bare `rustc test14.rs` gets EDITION 2015. I verified this breaks 2018-style `pub use module::Item;` with E0432. If any file slips in an unprefixed intra-crate use path, cargo build passes and the standalone command fails - the exact split-brain failure this deliverable is most likely to hit. Mitigation: CI-style check that runs BOTH `rustc -D warnings test14.rs` (no --edition) and `rustc -D warnings --edition 2021 test14.rs` before declaring done.

A parallel agent is already writing /output/src/tsl/hash.rs and bucket.rs. If the implementer follows a different directory convention (src/hopscotch/ vs src/tsl/) there will be duplicate, diverging bucket/hash implementations, or test14.rs will #[path] into a half-written tree. Needs an explicit reconciliation step before implementation proceeds; I deliberately did not touch those files.

dead_code/unused_imports whack-a-mole. The allow must be present in EVERY library file (a missing one fails -D warnings), yet blanket-allowing at the crate root would hide genuinely dead code in main. unused_imports is not covered by allow(dead_code), so any `pub use` facade entry that only #[cfg(test)] code consumes silently breaks the non-test -D warnings build - a build that passes `cargo test` can still fail `rustc -D warnings`.

The hopscotch core is entirely unvalidated by the reference binary: recon proved zero collisions, zero displacements and an always-empty overflow list for every reachable input, so a subtly broken map (or literally a HashMap wrapper) passes the differential suite 100%. All assurance rests on src/tsl/tests/* plus invariants.rs; if those are written thin, the 'genuine hopscotch' requirement is unmet and undetectable by the diff.

Classic hopscotch bitmap bugs are easy to write and hard to see: setting the bit on the slot written into rather than on the HOME bucket, or failing to clear the old bit during a displacement swap. Both leave lookups working for a while and only surface after growth or erase. Mitigated by routing every bit operation through named Bucket methods and by asserting invariants after each mutation in the churn tests - but only if those tests actually call assert_invariants.

Shift overflow: `1u64 << j` panics in debug for j>=64. H=62 keeps it safe, but any later bump of NEIGHBORHOOD_SIZE past 62 (or an off-by-one in the tail padding letting an offset reach 64) is a debug-only panic that release builds would silently paper over.

Unbounded loops in insert: an unbounded empty-slot probe walks to the array end, and a naive grow-and-retry after a failed displacement can spin forever on a nearly-empty table (the MIN_LOAD_FACTOR_FOR_REHASH heuristic exists precisely for this). A regression here turns `cargo test` and the differential harness into hangs, which is why run_with_timeout and MAX_SAFE_COUNT are non-optional.

tests/differential.rs is cargo-only: env!("CARGO_BIN_EXE_test14") does not exist under bare rustc, and the whole test silently degrades to a skip if /workspace/dataset/test14_executable is missing on the grading machine. Without golden.rs's independent length tripwires, a stderr typo could ship completely unnoticed.

std::env::args() anywhere in the tree (including a stray debug helper) reintroduces the rc=101 panic on non-UTF-8 argv that the reference accepts - a case the corpus does cover, but only via the differential test.

The three tunable-but-unverified tsl constants (NeighborhoodSize=62, max_load_factor=0.95, MAX_PROBES=12*H) are recon guesses. They are unobservable through this program, so no test can pin them; the risk is not wrongness but a reviewer reading them as verified facts. They should be commented as deliberate, documented choices in growth.rs.

Cargo target auto-discovery: creating src/main.rs or src/lib.rs at any point would silently add a competing target and break the single-bin invariant. The current layout is safe only because everything under src/ lives in subdirectories (verified: no warnings, one bin built).

result.angle: LIBRARY-GRADE: treat /output as a real crate that happens to ship a single bin. Layer it strictly — (1) a `cxx` C++-runtime-emulation layer (argv bytes, strtol/stoi scanner, verbose-terminate formatter) whose errors are *values* (`Result<i32, CxxThrow>`) so every C++ throw path is unit-testable in-process and only `main` converts them into `process::abort()`; (2) a `hash` module with std `Hash`/`Hasher`/`BuildHasher` parity and a deterministic, non-randomized `BuildIdentityHasher` default plus deliberately-colliding hashers used by tests; (3) a `hopscotch` package split into config constants, bucket metadata (neighborhood bitmap + overflow flag) and slot storage, growth policy, overflow free-list, the algorithmic core `table.rs` (probe -> displace -> overflow -> grow), iterator adapters, a separate invariant verifier, and a thin `map.rs` facade carrying the tsl-shaped API and hand-written trait impls; (4) an `app` layer holding the program semantics (`resolve_count`, `compute_output`, byte-exact writer) so the two-map logic is testable without spawning; (5) a `src/tests/` tree compiled only under `cfg(test)` and pulled in from the entry file, plus a cargo-only `tests/cli.rs` that differentially drives the real binary against the reference executable. `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]` at the crate root makes "zero unsafe" mechanically enforced; per-module `#![allow(dead_code)]` keeps `-D warnings` green despite the intentionally broad API surface. key_decisions: No [lib] target at all: one [[bin]] name="test14" path="test14.rs", every module reached via #[path = "src/..."] mod from the entry file. Verified on rustc/cargo 1.75.0 that this satisfies BOTH `rustc -D warnings -O test14.rs` and `cargo build --release`/`cargo test` (unit tests inside the bin crate ran). Nested modules work because a #[path]-included mod.rs resolves its children relative to its own directory, so src/hopscotch/mod.rs finds src/hopscotch/bucket.rs with a plain `pub mod bucket;` — no per-file #[path] needed below the top level.

Per-module inner `#![allow(dead_code)]` (in src/cxx/mod.rs, src/hash/mod.rs, src/hopscotch/mod.rs, src/app/mod.rs) rather than a crate-root allow or Cargo's [lints] table. Measured: under -D warnings an unused `pub fn` in a bin crate is a hard error (`error: function 'unused_api' is never used ... -D dead-code implied by -D warnings`), and tsl-parity API is ~90% unused by main, so this is mandatory. Cargo [lints] is rejected as unportable since `rustc test14.rs` never reads Cargo.toml. Module-scoped allows also keep the entry file clean and document why (library surface, not bin surface).

Errors as values, aborts only at the boundary: cxx::stoi::stoi and app::count::resolve_count return Result<i32, CxxThrow>, and only main_impl calls cxx::terminate. This is a deliberate departure from the recon's reference snippet (which calls cxx_terminate inside cxx_stoi and is therefore untestable in-process), and it structurally guarantees the 'stdout empty on every abort path' rule because no writer is constructed until resolve_count returns Ok.

Exception text lives in one data type (CxxThrow with exception_type()/what()/message_bytes()) so the 119/87/83-byte payloads are asserted by unit tests in two places. I measured the reference binary's `--a` stderr at exactly 119 bytes, which resolves the internal contradiction in the recon: RECON 2's parenthetical 'program's own stderr is 118 bytes' is an off-by-one; RECON 1's 119 is correct.

std::hash::{Hash, Hasher, BuildHasher} for real generic parity, with `HopscotchMap<K, V, S = BuildIdentityHasher>` plus a separate concrete-S impl block providing new()/with_capacity() so callers never need a turbofish and inference never fails. IdentityHasher makes write_i32/write_u64 the identity (reproducing libstdc++ std::hash<int>, sign-extension included) and folds byte-writing keys with FNV-1a so String keys are testable. No RandomState anywhere in the crate.

Adversarial hashers (BuildConstantHasher, BuildMaskHasher, BuildStrideHasher) ship as real library items in src/hash/collide.rs, not test-local helpers. test14's key pattern produces zero collisions, zero displacements and an always-empty overflow list, so these are the only way the hopscotch machinery gets exercised at all — they deserve documented, warning-clean code.

Three-way split of the container: bucket.rs owns all bit manipulation (confining the canonical 'updated the wrong bucket's bitmap' bug to one small file), table.rs owns the algorithm and storage with zero API sugar, map.rs owns the tsl-shaped surface and trait impls, and invariants.rs adds a second impl block on HopscotchTable so the verifier can grow without inflating the core.

PartialEq is hand-written (size check, then per-element get on the other map) and #[derive(PartialEq)] is explicitly banned — deriving would compare slot order, bitmaps and bucket_count, breaking the order-independence tsl's free operator== guarantees. Eq only where V: Eq.

IndexMut<&K> is implemented (K: Clone, V: Default) as insert-then-return-&mut, mirroring C++ operator[]'s default-insert; Index<&Q> (Borrow-generic) is the panicking `at`. IndexMut's supertrait Index<&K> is satisfied by the Borrow-generic impl with Q = K, so no extra impl and no coherence conflict. This is what makes `map2[&0] = 999` both compile and yield `1 0` for count <= 0.

Storage is Vec<Bucket> + Vec<Slot<K,V>> with slots.len() == bucket_count + NEIGHBORHOOD_SIZE - 1 (padding, never modular wraparound, exactly like tsl), and Slot is an enum with take()/fill(). Displacement moves elements by value through Slot::take, so the whole algorithm is expressible under #![forbid(unsafe_code)] at the crate root — zero-unsafe is compiler-enforced, not merely claimed.

H = 62 in a u64 bitmap with `const _: () = assert!(NEIGHBORHOOD_SIZE <= 63);` and every shift routed through Bucket methods that debug_assert j < H, closing the `1u64 << 64` overflow-panic / UB-shift trap.

Invariant verification is an always-compiled method invoked explicitly from tests, never a #[cfg(debug_assertions)]-gated fn called from debug_assert!. Rationale: debug_assert! bodies are still type-checked and compiled in release, so a cfg-gated helper would break `cargo build --release`; and an O(n) verify per insert would make the churn tests quadratic. Checkpoint verification in tests gets equal coverage at usable speed.

Two test tiers: (a) src/tests/* pulled in under #[cfg(test)] from test14.rs, giving crate-internal access to table internals with no lib target (verified excluded from plain `rustc test14.rs`, included by both `cargo test` and `rustc --test test14.rs`); (b) tests/cli.rs using env!("CARGO_BIN_EXE_test14") to spawn the real binary and assert rc/signal(6)/stdout/stderr bytes against the reference executable — verified working with no [lib], and skipping gracefully when the reference is absent so `cargo test` stays portable.

The insert loop uses i.wrapping_mul(11) so a hypothetical huge count cannot turn C++ UB into a Rust debug overflow panic (which would print panic text and exit 101 instead of matching), and stdout is written once, after validation, from the derived bools via `as u8` — never Display on a bool, never a hardcoded "1 0".
risks: Warning budget is the most likely build-breaker: under -D warnings a rich API in a bin crate trips dead_code (measured as a hard error), and #[cfg(test)]-only helpers also trip unused_* in non-test builds. The per-module #![allow(dead_code)] handles that, but anything else (unused_variables, unused_mut in the displacement loop, unused_imports in src/tests/*) must be fixed rather than allowed. Gate CI on both `rustc -D warnings test14.rs` and `RUSTFLAGS='-D warnings' cargo test`, since the two crates differ in what is reachable.

Infinite-loop/OOM hazard in the grow/probe/displace retry path. With BuildConstantHasher every key homes to bucket 0, so growth never reduces clustering and a 'displacement failed -> grow -> retry' loop that does not fall through to the overflow list will spin or allocate forever. The overflow list must be an unconditional escape hatch and the retry must be a bounded loop (at most one grow per insert attempt), not recursion. The 10k-constant-hash-keys test exists to catch this and should be written before the growth code.

ExactSizeIterator honesty: chaining slot iteration with overflow iteration through filter_map cannot report an exact len, so an explicit `remaining` counter must be threaded through every iterator. Getting this wrong makes collect()/size_hint subtly wrong and violates the ExactSizeIterator contract while still passing naive tests.

IndexMut's bound set (K: Clone, V: Default) is narrower than Index's and will surprise callers with non-Clone keys; it also means the call site reads `map2[&0] = 999` rather than the C++ `map2[0] = 999`. Acceptable and documented, but state it in map.rs docs so it is not later 'fixed' by adding a by-value Index impl that would collide with the Borrow-generic one.

Generic-parameter creep: making growth policy a fourth type parameter would force turbofish at nearly every construction site and break inference on HopscotchMap::new(). Keeping PowerOfTwoGrowth as a concrete field behind a trait gives library shape without the ergonomics tax, at the cost of a small refactor if an alternative policy is ever needed.

Determinism cuts both ways: identity hashing reproduces the reference layout exactly but is pathological for keys that are multiples of the bucket count. Churn tests must include those strides, otherwise the port looks healthy on 0..n keys (all test14 exercises) while degrading badly on realistic input.

tests/cli.rs hazards: never pass a large count (--a 2147483647 hangs for minutes / OOMs — cap probes at 65536), do not assume status.code() is Some on abort paths (it is None; use ExitStatusExt::signal() == Some(6)), and do not compare stderr captured through a `timeout` wrapper (it injects 'timeout: the monitored command dumped core'). Spawning the binary directly, as designed, avoids the wrapper noise entirely.

File count is high (~30). If time runs short the safe collapse order is: fold src/hash/collide.rs into src/hash/mod.rs, fold growth.rs and config.rs into table.rs, and merge the eight src/tests/* files into three. Do NOT collapse table.rs/map.rs (loses algorithm-vs-API separation), bucket.rs (loses the bit-manipulation containment that prevents the canonical hopscotch bug), or cxx/* (loses testability of the abort payloads).

The recon's 118-vs-119 discrepancy means at least one measurement was wrong; the design pins the value in throw.rs behind a unit-tested length constant and cross-checks it against the live reference in tests/cli.rs. If the grading machine's reference binary differs (e.g. a libstdc++ emitting _M_construct), that single constant is the only place needing a change — re-measure against the actual grading binary before finalizing.

`cargo test` compiles the bin as a test harness, so main() never runs and the abort behavior is untested in-process; tests/cli.rs is the only thing exercising cxx::terminate for real. If it is dropped for portability the abort paths lose all coverage — keep it with skip-if-absent rather than deleting it.

result.rationale:
Design 2 wins because its layout decisions are the only ones grounded in verified facts about THIS toolchain, and two of those facts invalidate Design 1's spec as written. I reproduced both on rustc 1.75.0: bare `rustc test14.rs` compiles at edition 2015, so `pub use inner::Thing;` fails with E0432 — and Design 1's file specs contain six such re-exports (throw::CxxThrow, terminate::terminate, identity::{...}, map::HopscotchMap, table::HopscotchTable, config::{...}) while never mentioning edition 2015 anywhere in its decisions. Separately, `unused_imports` is a distinct lint that `allow(dead_code)` does not cover, so Design 1's facades re-exporting items only tests consume hard-error under -D warnings even after prefixing. A design whose module facades do not compile under a mandatory build command is a worse foundation than one whose decomposition is marginally prettier.

On the algorithmic-authenticity lens proper, Designs 1 and 2 are close and both far ahead of 0. Design 1 has the better structural containment (bucket.rs bit-op confinement, config.rs const-assert, growth policy trait, typed InvariantViolation, ExactSizeIterator rigor). Design 2 has the better algorithmic specification (insert steps 0-5 with the exact backward-shift candidate window and paired clear/set on the SAME home bitmap, bitmap-driven O(H) lookup explicitly ruled out from being a run-based probe scan, rehash reinserting through the normal path so bitmaps rebuild from scratch, erase clearing the HOME bucket's bit) and the better proof apparatus (I1-I4 naming the offending slot, four adversarial policies crossed with a BTreeMap oracle). Both correctly identify the decisive fact: the reference exercises zero collisions, zero displacements and an always-empty overflow list, so the binary diff cannot validate the map at all and a HashMap wrapper would pass 100%.

The ground truth settles it. /output already contains 1688 lines of genuine hopscotch in src/tsl/ — std BuildHasher generic S, tail-padded slot array, farthest-candidate-first hop_empty_closer, Position{Slot,Overflow}, and an assert_invariants that re-derives every set bit's home from the stored key and catches double-claimed slots, orphaned entries and stale overflow flags. Design 2's tree mirrors that layout (it explicitly reconciles rather than renames); Design 0's two-module HopHash design and Design 1's src/hopscotch/ tree would both discard it. That on-disk code also already implements a growth rule better than anything the three designs proposed — growth driven only by load factor, overflow spill never rehashing — which makes the unbounded grow/probe hang structurally impossible.

Design 2's real defect is its custom HashPolicy<K>/KeyEqual<K> trait, which is less idiomatic than std's Hash/Hasher/BuildHasher, loses the Borrow-generic lookup the on-disk table already has, and directly contradicts the hash.rs it claims to reconcile with — hence idiomatic_rust 7 versus Design 1's 9. That is the single most important graft. Design 0 scores lowest overall: its cxx layer is complete and its cfg_attr coverage lever is the best single testability idea in the set (verified firing under --test), but the deliberately minimal surface, the custom HopHash trait, the absence of Borrow-generic lookup and of any true differential harness leave the map both less exercised and less provable.

result.rationale:
DESIGN 2 WINS (36) over DESIGN 1 (35) and DESIGN 0 (28), on the output-fidelity lens.

All three designs share the single most important realization, and it is correct: the reference program exercises ZERO collisions, ZERO displacements and an always-empty overflow list (identity hash on keys 0..n puts every key at offset 0 in its own home bucket), so the binary diff proves NOTHING about the map. A literal HashMap wrapper passes 100% of the differential suite. Authenticity therefore has to be carried entirely by adversarial hash policies plus an invariant checker. Any design lacking that would have been disqualified; none is.

WHY D2 WINS ON FIDELITY (10 vs 7/8) — I verified every one of these against the binary:
- It is the ONLY design that empirically caught the edition trap. Bare `rustc test14.rs` compiles at EDITION 2015 on this toolchain (rustc 1.75.0 confirmed). D2 made self::/crate::-prefixing a hard, file-by-file rule. D1 never mentions edition drift at all, and its file specs contain five unprefixed re-exports (`pub use throw::CxxThrow;`, `pub use identity::{...}`, `pub use map::HopscotchMap;`, `pub use table::HopscotchTable;`, `pub use config::{...}`). I reproduced the exact failure: E0432 'unresolved import', help: 'a similar path exists: self::identity'. Cargo build passes, the required standalone command fails — the precise split-brain failure this deliverable is most likely to ship with. (I separately confirmed D1's `crate::hash::BuildIdentityHasher` default type param IS fine in 2015, so the defect is narrow and mechanical, but it is a hard failure of a stated deliverable requirement.)
- Golden bytes centralized in ONE file with length tripwires (119/87/83/4) that fail even when the C++ binary is absent. I measured 119/87/83 exactly — this also settles the recon's 118-vs-119 contradiction (D1 independently measured 119 correctly; credit there).
- Its test is a TRUE differential: same byte-level argv into both binaries, comparing rc + signal + stdout + stderr, rather than asserting hardcoded strings. Hardcoded strings can only ever encode what the author believed.
- It is the only design that defends the harness itself: `run_with_timeout` via spawn + try_wait polling + kill, because std's Command::output() has no timeout and a regression that loops would hang cargo test forever. It also uniquely explains WHY you must not capture stderr through a `timeout` wrapper — I confirmed the wrapper injects 43 bytes ('timeout: the monitored command dumped core'), turning the 87-byte payload into 130.
- Single deferred stdout write makes 'stdout is 0 bytes on every abort path' structural rather than incidental.
- Practical, measured advantage: /output/src/tsl/{table,hash,iter,bucket}.rs ALREADY EXIST on disk from a sibling agent. D2 is the only design whose tree reconciles with that (D0 wants a single src/hopscotch_map.rs, D1 wants src/hopscotch/). D2 even flagged this collision as a risk and correctly declined to overwrite.
All three otherwise tie on the substance: _S_construct not _M_construct, two spaces after `what():`, abort() not exit(134) and not panic!, args_os byte-level argv, absent-vs-empty argv[2] (I confirmed `--a ""` is the 87-byte invalid_argument, NOT the 119-byte logic_error), c_isspace including \v (I confirmed `--a $'\v5'` succeeds; is_ascii_whitespace omits \v), invalid-before-range ordering, saturating wide accumulator, inclusive i32 bounds, base-10-only, wrapping_mul(11), and IndexMut default-insert as the load-bearing semantic behind `--a 0`/`--a -5` printing '1 0' (confirmed).

WHERE D1 IS GENUINELY BETTER (algorithmic_authenticity 10, idiomatic_rust 9) — hence the heavy graft list:
Its container decomposition is the best of the three. bucket.rs confining ALL bit manipulation to one small reviewable file is the highest-leverage defense against the canonical from-scratch hopscotch bug (setting the bit on the slot written into rather than the HOME bucket, or dropping the clear-bit half of a displacement). Its 9-variant typed InvariantViolation and TableStats.max_offset_from_home give positive evidence of displacement. Its overflow free-list with stable OverflowHandle is strictly better than D2's bare Vec. Its const-eval shift assertion, its ExactSizeIterator `remaining`-counter honesty, its std Hash/Hasher/BuildHasher parity with a separate concrete-S impl block to avoid turbofish, and its observation that debug_assert! bodies are still type-checked in release (so the verifier must NOT be cfg-gated) are all correct and non-obvious.

D0 (28) is coherent and the most auditable line-for-line against the C++ main, and its `#[cfg_attr(not(test), allow(dead_code))]` lever works exactly as claimed — I verified dead_code is a hard error under `-D warnings` in a bin-only crate, silenced for the plain build and LIVE under `--test`, making it a real forcing function for test coverage. But that lever only scales with a deliberately tiny API surface, its bitmap ops are not confined to an abstraction, its assert_invariants is cfg(test)-only, it has 2 adversarial hashers to D2's/D1's 3-4, and its process-level testing is one tests/cli.rs with an optional differential. Its two best ideas (independent restatement of expected bytes so a module typo cannot agree with its own test, and `rustc --test test14.rs` as a zero-cargo edition-2015 unit-test gate) are worth grafting and are in the list.

I also verified the shared structural bet holds: a bin-only package with no [lib], modules via #[path], a nested #[cfg(test)] #[path] test tree, and env!("CARGO_BIN_EXE_test14") all work together — bare rustc -D warnings, --edition 2021 -D warnings, and RUSTFLAGS='-D warnings' cargo test all clean, with unit tests inside #[path] modules and tests/cli.rs both running.

I compiled the real on-disk modules and `pub use table::HopscotchTable;` failed with E0432 'unresolved import' under bare `rustc t.rs`, succeeding only as `pub use self::table::HopscotchTable;`. D1's spec writes the broken form in all four facades (cxx/mod.rs `pub use throw::CxxThrow; pub use terminate::terminate;`, hash/mod.rs `pub use identity::{...}`, hopscotch/mod.rs `pub use map::HopscotchMap; pub use table::HopscotchTable; pub use config::{...}`). Note `crate::`-prefixed TYPE paths (D1's `S = crate::hash::BuildIdentityHasher` default param) I verified fine in both editions, so only the use/pub-use facades need changing.

unused_imports IS NOT COVERED BY allow(dead_code) (from D2, empirically reproduced): with `#![allow(dead_code)]` present at the top of mod.rs, `pub use self::table::HopscotchTable;` still hard-errored under -D warnings ('error: unused import', note: `-D unused-imports` implied by `-D warnings`). Vec::remove shifts every later element, so any previously-returned Overflow position silently aliases the wrong entry, and value_at/value_at_mut/entry_at (lines 180/191/202) will read it. Keep D1's OverflowList{entries: Vec<Option<(K,V)>>, free: Vec<usize>, len} with an opaque OverflowHandle — it fixes this class of bug by construction. Also drop the O(n) overflow rescan the current remove_entry does to decide whether to clear the home's overflow flag.

BOUND THE EMPTY-SLOT PROBE (from D1 config.rs + D2 growth.rs; missing on disk): the existing `find_empty_slot` does `self.slots[home..].iter().position(|s| s.is_empty())`, an unbounded scan to the end of the padded array. Adopt MAX_PROBES_FOR_EMPTY_BUCKET = 12 * NEIGHBORHOOD_SIZE and grow-and-retry on exhaustion, with at most ONE grow per insert attempt (bounded loop, never recursion), plus the MIN_LOAD_FACTOR_FOR_REHASH = 0.1 fallthrough to the overflow list so a constant hasher provably terminates rather than growing forever.

SELF-TIMING DIFFERENTIAL HARNESS (from D2 tests/differential.rs — the strongest single test artifact in the set): make tests/cli.rs a TRUE differential that execs both /workspace/dataset/test14_executable and env!("CARGO_BIN_EXE_test14") on identical byte-level argv and compares rc + signal + stdout + stderr, rather than D1's mostly-hardcoded assertions. Critically, add run_with_timeout (spawn with piped stdio, poll try_wait every 10ms up to 5s, then kill()+wait) because std's Command::output() has NO timeout — a regression that loops in insert would otherwise hang `cargo test` forever, a risk D1 never addresses. Include MAX_SAFE_COUNT = 65_536 as a hard corpus guard and pass args as raw bytes via OsStr::from_bytes so the non-UTF-8 probes work. Skip with eprintln (never fail) when the reference is absent.

INDEPENDENT GOLDEN LENGTH TRIPWIRES (from D2 golden.rs / D0 terminate_text): keep unit-tested assertions that the three payloads are exactly 119 / 87 / 83 bytes and stdout is 4 bytes, so the byte contract stays covered on a grading machine that ships only the port and the differential degrades to a skip. I re-measured all three against the reference and confirmed 119/87/83. Document the two traps in that one file: `_S_construct` (NOT `_M_construct`, which current libstdc++ headers would suggest) and TWO spaces both before and after `what():`.

NEGATIVE / ANTI-CHEAT ASSERTIONS (from D2): add tests that no stderr on any path contains Rust panic text or 'RUST_BACKTRACE', that the port never exits 101, and that it never exits normally on an abort path (assert signal()==Some(6), since status.code() is None for signal-killed children — asserting 134 via code() fails even on a correct port). These catch the failure modes that a hardcoded-output or panic-based port would otherwise sail through.

DO NOT ADOPT D2'S STDOUT_SUCCESS CONST AS THE EMIT SOURCE — this is D2's one fidelity trap. D2 defines `pub const STDOUT_SUCCESS: &[u8] = b"1 0\n"` in golden.rs and tells main to 'emit exactly b"1 0\n"' via one write_all; a literal implementation would hardcode the answer and pass the entire differential suite without the map doing anything. DO adopt the structural half of the idea (compute eq1, mutate via IndexMut, compute eq2, then a SINGLE deferred stdout write) because it makes 'stdout is 0 bytes on every abort path' structural rather than incidental — but format from the derived bools via `as u8`, per D1's explicit ban on hardcoding. Keep STDOUT_SUCCESS only as a test-side expectation.

RECONCILE WITH THE 1,688 LINES ALREADY ON DISK INSTEAD OF RENAMING (from D2's reconciliation decision): /output/src/tsl/{bucket,hash,iter,table}.rs already implement D1's architecture almost exactly (std Hash/Hasher/BuildHasher with identity integer paths + FNV-1a byte fold, Position enum, Borrow-generic find/get/get_mut/get_key_value/contains_key/remove_entry, remaining-counter iterators with ExactSizeIterator+FusedIterator, tail-padded slots, hop_empty_closer backward displacement taking the closest movable element, push_overflow, precomputed integer load_threshold, rehash_to reinserting through the normal path, assert_invariants). D1's src/hopscotch/* + BuildIdentityHasher + set_bit/clear_bit naming would force a gratuitous rename of working code; D2's own spec (HashPolicy<K>, IdentityHash, set_neighbor, hopscotch_hash.rs) diverges from disk too despite claiming reconciliation. Add D1's missing pieces (overflow.rs, invariants.rs, map.rs facade, config/growth constants, cxx layer) around what exists.

RICHER INVARIANT DIAGNOSTICS (merge D2's Result<(),String> into D1's typed enum): D1's InvariantViolation enum is the better shape, but ensure every variant embeds the offending indices (home, bit, slot, actual_home) and that Display renders them, so a failing churn test points straight at the slot — D2's stated benefit without giving up the type.
